title: String functions
summary_md: Exact syntax and argument order for the string functions interviewers use, with MySQL and SQL Server side by side: concatenation, length, substring, search, trim/pad, splitting, aggregation and cleaning.

sections.heading: Joining strings: CONCAT, CONCAT_WS, +
sections.body_md:
- `CONCAT(a, b, ...)` works in both engines and converts numbers to text. NULL handling differs (see the NULL page): MySQL returns NULL, SQL Server treats NULL as empty.
- `CONCAT_WS(sep, a, b, ...)` puts `sep` between values and **skips NULLs**. Position 1 is the separator, not data.
- SQL Server also has `a + b`; both sides must be text (`'ID-' + 5` fails - use `CONCAT` or `CAST`). NULL + anything = NULL.
- MySQL has **no** string `+` (it adds numbers) and `||` means OR unless `PIPES_AS_CONCAT` is set.

syntax.tsql:
CONCAT(str1, str2 [, ...])
CONCAT_WS(separator, str1, str2 [, ...])   -- 2017+
str1 + str2

args.name: separator (CONCAT_WS position 1)
args.meaning: Text placed between the remaining arguments.

args.name: str1, str2, ...
args.meaning: Values to join, in order. Non-text values are converted.

examples.title: CONCAT and CONCAT_WS with literals
examples.explain_md: Numbers are converted automatically; `CONCAT_WS` inserts the separator only between values.
examples.mysql: SELECT CONCAT('order-', 7) AS tagged, CONCAT_WS('/', '2024', '03', '15') AS path, CONCAT('a', 'b', 'c') AS abc;
examples.tsql: SELECT CONCAT('order-', 7) AS tagged, CONCAT_WS('/', '2024', '03', '15') AS path, CONCAT('a', 'b', 'c') AS abc;

examples.title: Build a label from a column
examples.explain_md: `CONCAT` accepts the INT `order_id` directly in both engines. The SQL Server `+` operator would need `CAST(order_id AS VARCHAR(10))`.
examples.mysql: SELECT order_id, CONCAT('ORD-', order_id, ' (', status, ')') AS label FROM orders WHERE order_id <= 103 ORDER BY order_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT order_id, 'ORD-' + CAST(order_id AS VARCHAR(10)) + ' (' + status + ')' AS label FROM orders WHERE order_id <= 103 ORDER BY order_id;

sections.heading: Length: LENGTH vs CHAR_LENGTH vs LEN vs DATALENGTH
sections.body_md:
Four names, three behaviours.
- MySQL `CHAR_LENGTH(s)` = number of **characters**, trailing spaces included. MySQL `LENGTH(s)` = number of **bytes** (a multi-byte character such as an accented letter counts 2+ in utf8mb4). Use CHAR_LENGTH for 'how long is this text'.
- SQL Server `LEN(s)` = characters, but **ignores trailing spaces**. `DATALENGTH(s)` = bytes **including** trailing spaces (NVARCHAR uses 2 bytes per character, so divide by 2).
- Trick for trailing spaces in SQL Server: `LEN(s + 'x') - 1`.
- NULL in, NULL out (all four).
- Use length to find dirty data: `WHERE LEN(col) <> LEN(TRIM(col))` (SQL Server) / `WHERE CHAR_LENGTH(col) <> CHAR_LENGTH(TRIM(col))` (MySQL).

syntax.tsql:
LEN(str)          -- characters, ignores trailing spaces
DATALENGTH(expr)  -- bytes

args.name: str
args.meaning: The text to measure.

examples.title: Trailing spaces
examples.explain_md: The literal has two trailing spaces: 5 characters, 3 after trimming. SQL Server `LEN` already ignores them (3); `DATALENGTH` counts them (5).
examples.mysql: SELECT CHAR_LENGTH('abc  ') AS with_trailing, CHAR_LENGTH(TRIM('abc  ')) AS ignoring_trailing;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATALENGTH('abc  ') AS with_trailing, LEN('abc  ') AS ignoring_trailing;
examples.dialect_note_md: MySQL: `CHAR_LENGTH('abc  ')` is 5 and `LENGTH` is the byte count (5 for ASCII). SQL Server: `LEN('abc  ')` is 3, `DATALENGTH('abc  ')` is 5 for VARCHAR (10 for NVARCHAR).

examples.title: Spot the dirty email
examples.explain_md: Customers 4 and 6 are 'the same' address in different case; customer 6 also has a trailing space, so it is one character longer.
examples.mysql: SELECT customer_id, email, CHAR_LENGTH(email) AS chars, CHAR_LENGTH(TRIM(email)) AS chars_trimmed FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (4, 6) ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT customer_id, email, DATALENGTH(email) AS chars, LEN(email) AS chars_trimmed FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (4, 6) ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: In SQL Server `DATALENGTH` on a VARCHAR column equals the character count including trailing spaces, and `LEN` skips the trailing space.

sections.heading: SUBSTRING, LEFT, RIGHT, REVERSE (1-based positions)
sections.body_md:
Positions start at **1**, not 0.
- `SUBSTRING(str, start, length)`: position 1 = the string, position 2 = first character to take (1-based), position 3 = how many characters (optional in MySQL; **required** in SQL Server - pass a big number such as `8000` for 'to the end').
- MySQL accepts a **negative start**: `SUBSTRING('interview', -4)` counts from the right = `view`. SQL Server has no such rule (use `RIGHT`).
- `start = 0`: MySQL returns an empty string. SQL Server treats 0 as 'one before the string' so the window is shifted: `SUBSTRING('interview', 0, 3)` = `in`.
- `LEFT(str, n)` / `RIGHT(str, n)`: first / last n characters, same in both engines.
- `REVERSE(str)` exists in both; palindromes and 'last token' tricks use it.
- MySQL aliases: `SUBSTR`, `MID`, `SUBSTRING(str FROM start FOR length)`.

syntax.mysql:
SUBSTRING(str, start [, length])
LEFT(str, n)
RIGHT(str, n)
REVERSE(str)
syntax.tsql:
SUBSTRING(expression, start, length)
LEFT(expression, n)
RIGHT(expression, n)
REVERSE(expression)

args.name: str / expression (position 1)
args.meaning: The text to cut.

args.name: start (position 2)
args.meaning: 1-based index of the first character kept. MySQL: negative counts from the end.

args.name: length (position 3)
args.meaning: How many characters to return. Optional in MySQL; required in SQL Server.

args.name: n (LEFT/RIGHT position 2)
args.meaning: Number of characters from the left / right edge.

examples.title: Extract pieces
examples.explain_md: `SUBSTRING('interview', 2, 4)` starts at the 2nd letter and takes 4: `nter`. LEFT/RIGHT take from either end.
examples.mysql: SELECT SUBSTRING('interview', 2, 4) AS mid, SUBSTRING('interview', 6) AS tail, LEFT('interview', 3) AS first3, RIGHT('interview', 4) AS last4, REVERSE('interview') AS reversed;
examples.tsql: SELECT SUBSTRING('interview', 2, 4) AS mid, SUBSTRING('interview', 6, 8000) AS tail, LEFT('interview', 3) AS first3, RIGHT('interview', 4) AS last4, REVERSE('interview') AS reversed;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server requires the third argument of SUBSTRING, so 'to the end' is written with a large length.

examples.title: Counting from the right
examples.explain_md: MySQL accepts a negative start (position 2): -4 means 'the 4th character from the end'. SQL Server computes the position instead.
examples.mysql: SELECT SUBSTRING('interview', -4, 4) AS negative_start, SUBSTRING('interview', -4) AS negative_to_end;
examples.tsql: SELECT SUBSTRING('interview', LEN('interview') - 3, 4) AS negative_start, SUBSTRING('interview', LEN('interview') - 3, 8000) AS negative_to_end;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server has no negative-start form; `RIGHT('interview', 4)` is the shortcut. Also note `SUBSTRING('interview', 0, 3)` returns `in` in SQL Server (the window begins one position before the string) but an empty string in MySQL.

examples.title: Initial and first 5 letters of email
examples.explain_md: Typical report columns built from `LEFT` and `SUBSTRING`.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, LEFT(name, 1) AS initial, SUBSTRING(email, 1, 5) AS email_start FROM customers WHERE customer_id <= 3 ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, LEFT(name, 1) AS initial, SUBSTRING(email, 1, 5) AS email_start FROM customers WHERE customer_id <= 3 ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.heading: Finding text: LOCATE / INSTR vs CHARINDEX
sections.body_md:
All return the **1-based position** of the first match, or **0** if not found. The argument order differs - the classic interview slip:
- MySQL `LOCATE(substr, str [, start])` - needle first.
- MySQL `INSTR(str, substr)` - haystack first (no start argument). `POSITION(substr IN str)` is the standard spelling of LOCATE.
- SQL Server `CHARINDEX(substr, str [, start])` - needle first, like LOCATE.
- `start` (position 3) is 1-based: the search begins at that character, and the returned position is still counted from the start of the whole string.
- All three are case-insensitive under the default collations. For 'contains', `col LIKE '%x%'` is simpler.
- SQL Server `PATINDEX('%pattern%', str)` supports wildcards; MySQL needs `REGEXP` for that.

args.name: substr
args.meaning: The text to look for (LOCATE/CHARINDEX position 1; INSTR position 2).

args.name: str
args.meaning: The text to search in (LOCATE/CHARINDEX position 2; INSTR position 1).

args.name: start
args.meaning: Optional 1-based position to begin searching (LOCATE/CHARINDEX position 3). Default 1.

examples.title: Position of '@'
examples.explain_md: `LOCATE` and `CHARINDEX` take the needle first; `INSTR` flips it. All give 5.
examples.mysql: SELECT LOCATE('@', 'maya@shop.com') AS locate_pos, INSTR('maya@shop.com', '@') AS instr_pos, LOCATE('o', 'maya@shop.com', 8) AS second_o, LOCATE('z', 'maya@shop.com') AS missing;
examples.tsql: SELECT CHARINDEX('@', 'maya@shop.com') AS locate_pos, CHARINDEX('@', 'maya@shop.com') AS instr_pos, CHARINDEX('o', 'maya@shop.com', 8) AS second_o, CHARINDEX('z', 'maya@shop.com') AS missing;

examples.title: Where is the '@' in each email?
examples.explain_md: Same call over a column; useful as the building block for splitting at the delimiter.
examples.mysql: SELECT customer_id, email, LOCATE('@', email) AS at_pos FROM customers ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT customer_id, email, CHARINDEX('@', email) AS at_pos FROM customers ORDER BY customer_id;

pitfalls_md: INSTR and LOCATE have the arguments in opposite orders; CHARINDEX copies LOCATE. Swap them and you silently get 0.

sections.heading: REPLACE, TRIM, UPPER/LOWER, padding
sections.body_md:
- `REPLACE(str, from, to)`: replaces every occurrence. MySQL matches **case-sensitively**; SQL Server follows the column collation (case-insensitive by default).
- `TRIM(str)` strips spaces both sides in both engines. `LTRIM` / `RTRIM` strip one side. MySQL: `TRIM([BOTH|LEADING|TRAILING] chars FROM str)`; SQL Server 2017+: `TRIM(chars FROM str)` - there `chars` is a **set** of characters to strip.
- `UPPER(str)` / `LOWER(str)` are the same in both.
- Zero-padding: MySQL `LPAD(str, len, pad)` / `RPAD(...)`. **LPAD truncates** from the right if `str` is longer than `len`. SQL Server has no LPAD: use `RIGHT(CONCAT(REPLICATE('0', n), str), n)` (or `FORMAT(num, '00000')`); `RIGHT` keeps the *last* n characters, so truncation drops the left.
- `REPEAT(str, n)` (MySQL) = `REPLICATE(str, n)` (SQL Server).

syntax.mysql:
REPLACE(str, from_str, to_str)
TRIM([{BOTH|LEADING|TRAILING} [remstr] FROM] str)
LPAD(str, len, padstr)
RPAD(str, len, padstr)
syntax.tsql:
REPLACE(string, pattern, replacement)
TRIM([characters FROM] string)
RIGHT(CONCAT(REPLICATE(pad, len), str), len)   -- LPAD
LEFT(CONCAT(str, REPLICATE(pad, len)), len)    -- RPAD

args.name: str / string (REPLACE position 1)
args.meaning: The text to search.

args.name: from_str (position 2)
args.meaning: Text to find (all occurrences).

args.name: to_str (position 3)
args.meaning: Replacement; '' deletes the match.

args.name: len (LPAD position 2)
args.meaning: Final length of the result (longer input is cut to this length).

args.name: padstr (LPAD position 3)
args.meaning: Characters used to fill on the left (LPAD) or right (RPAD).

examples.title: REPLACE and TRIM
examples.explain_md: Remove dashes, strip spaces, strip a specific character from both ends.
examples.mysql: SELECT REPLACE('555-123-4567', '-', '') AS digits, TRIM('  hello  ') AS trimmed, TRIM(BOTH 'x' FROM 'xxhixx') AS stripped_x, UPPER('mixed Case') AS up, LOWER('MIXED Case') AS low;
examples.tsql: SELECT REPLACE('555-123-4567', '-', '') AS digits, TRIM('  hello  ') AS trimmed, TRIM(BOTH 'x' FROM 'xxhixx') AS stripped_x, UPPER('mixed Case') AS up, LOWER('MIXED Case') AS low;
examples.dialect_note_md: `TRIM(BOTH chars FROM str)` needs SQL Server 2017+ (the BOTH keyword is optional there).

examples.title: REPLACE is case-sensitive in MySQL only
examples.explain_md: MySQL leaves 'AbA' untouched because 'a' is not 'A'.
examples.mysql: SELECT REPLACE('AbA', 'a', '-') AS result;
examples.tsql: SELECT REPLACE('AbA', 'a', '-') AS result;
examples.dialect_note_md: Real SQL Server (default case-insensitive collation) returns `-b-`; MySQL returns `AbA`. Force a case-sensitive match with `COLLATE Latin1_General_CS_AS` on the first argument.

examples.title: Zero-pad order ids to 6 digits
examples.explain_md: `LPAD(7, 6, '0')` style padding. SQL Server builds it from REPLICATE and RIGHT.
examples.mysql: SELECT order_id, LPAD(order_id, 6, '0') AS padded FROM orders WHERE order_id IN (101, 114) ORDER BY order_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT order_id, RIGHT(CONCAT(REPLICATE('0', 6), order_id), 6) AS padded FROM orders WHERE order_id IN (101, 114) ORDER BY order_id;

pitfalls_md: `LPAD('12345', 3, '0')` returns `123` (cuts the right side); the `RIGHT(...)` idiom in SQL Server returns `345`. Check max length before padding.
MySQL `TRIM('xy' FROM s)` strips the exact substring 'xy'; SQL Server's `TRIM('xy' FROM s)` strips any of the characters x or y.

sections.heading: Text before / after a delimiter
sections.body_md:
Classic tasks: email domain, local part, first name, last word.
- MySQL: `SUBSTRING_INDEX(str, delim, count)`. Position 3 `count` > 0 returns everything **before** the count-th delimiter from the left; `count` < 0 returns everything **after** the |count|-th delimiter from the right. If the delimiter is absent, the whole string comes back.
- Domain: `SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1)`. Local part: `SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', 1)`. Nth item: nest two calls: `SUBSTRING_INDEX(SUBSTRING_INDEX(s, ',', n), ',', -1)`.
- SQL Server has no equivalent: combine `CHARINDEX` with `LEFT` / `SUBSTRING`. Before the delimiter: `LEFT(s, CHARINDEX(d, s) - 1)`; after: `SUBSTRING(s, CHARINDEX(d, s) + 1, 8000)`.
- If the delimiter is missing, `CHARINDEX` = 0 and `LEFT(s, -1)` raises an error. Guard: `LEFT(s, CHARINDEX(d, s + d) - 1)`.
- Last word in SQL Server: `RIGHT(s, CHARINDEX(' ', REVERSE(s)) - 1)`.
- SQL Server 2022 adds `STRING_SPLIT(s, sep, 1)` with an ordinal column for 'Nth item'.

syntax.tsql:
LEFT(str, CHARINDEX(delim, str) - 1)
SUBSTRING(str, CHARINDEX(delim, str) + 1, 8000)

args.name: str (position 1)
args.meaning: The text to split.

args.name: delim (position 2)
args.meaning: The delimiter; case-sensitive, may be longer than one character.

args.name: count (position 3)
args.meaning: Which delimiter counts. +n: everything before the nth delimiter from the left. -n: everything after the nth delimiter from the right.

examples.title: Local part and domain
examples.explain_md: `SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1)` is the text after the last '@'. Trimming first removes customer 6's trailing space.
examples.mysql: SELECT customer_id, SUBSTRING_INDEX(TRIM(email), '@', 1) AS local_part, SUBSTRING_INDEX(TRIM(email), '@', -1) AS domain FROM customers ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT customer_id, LEFT(TRIM(email), CHARINDEX('@', TRIM(email)) - 1) AS local_part, SUBSTRING(TRIM(email), CHARINDEX('@', TRIM(email)) + 1, 8000) AS domain FROM customers ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: First and last name
examples.explain_md: Positive count = left side of the first space; negative count = right side of the last space.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, SUBSTRING_INDEX(name, ' ', 1) AS first_name, SUBSTRING_INDEX(name, ' ', -1) AS last_name FROM customers WHERE customer_id <= 3 ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, LEFT(name, CHARINDEX(' ', name) - 1) AS first_name, SUBSTRING(name, CHARINDEX(' ', name) + 1, 8000) AS last_name FROM customers WHERE customer_id <= 3 ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: Third item of a comma list (MySQL nesting)
examples.explain_md: Inner call keeps 'a,b,c'; outer call with -1 keeps what follows the last comma: `c`.
examples.mysql: SELECT SUBSTRING_INDEX(SUBSTRING_INDEX('a,b,c,d', ',', 3), ',', -1) AS third_item, SUBSTRING_INDEX('no-delimiter', ',', 1) AS missing_delim;
examples.tsql: SELECT SUBSTRING('a,b,c,d', 5, 1) AS third_item, LEFT('no-delimiter', CHARINDEX(',', 'no-delimiter' + ',') - 1) AS missing_delim;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server has no nth-item helper for fixed positions; the literal `SUBSTRING('a,b,c,d', 5, 1)` just shows the result. In practice use `STRING_SPLIT(s, ',', 1)` (2022+) or split with a numbers table.

sections.heading: Aggregating text: GROUP_CONCAT vs STRING_AGG
sections.body_md:
- MySQL `GROUP_CONCAT([DISTINCT] expr [ORDER BY expr [ASC|DESC]] [SEPARATOR 'sep'])`. Default separator is a comma. Output is silently truncated at `group_concat_max_len` (1024 bytes by default).
- SQL Server 2017+ `STRING_AGG(expr, separator) [WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY expr)]`. The separator is **required**; there is **no DISTINCT** (dedupe in a subquery first).
- Without an ORDER BY the element order is unspecified in both - add one for deterministic output.
- Both skip NULL values; if all inputs are NULL the result is NULL.
- SQL Server `STRING_AGG` returns NVARCHAR(4000)/VARCHAR(8000) unless the input is MAX; cast to `VARCHAR(MAX)` for long lists.

args.name: expr (position 1)
args.meaning: The column or expression to concatenate.

args.name: separator
args.meaning: MySQL: after the SEPARATOR keyword, default ','. SQL Server: position 2, required.

examples.title: People per department
examples.explain_md: Names sorted inside each group, joined with a comma and a space.
examples.mysql: SELECT dept, GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY name SEPARATOR ', ') AS people FROM employees GROUP BY dept ORDER BY dept;
examples.tsql: SELECT dept, STRING_AGG(name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY name) AS people FROM employees GROUP BY dept ORDER BY dept;

examples.title: Distinct list
examples.explain_md: MySQL has DISTINCT inside GROUP_CONCAT; SQL Server needs a DISTINCT subquery.
examples.mysql: SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT dept ORDER BY dept SEPARATOR '|') AS depts FROM employees;
examples.tsql: SELECT STRING_AGG(dept, '|') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY dept) AS depts FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM employees) AS d;

sections.heading: Cleaning text and case-insensitive comparison
sections.body_md:
- Default collations (MySQL `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`, SQL Server `SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS`) compare text **case-insensitively**: `'ABC' = 'abc'` is TRUE and `LIKE` ignores case. `GROUP BY` and `DISTINCT` also merge them.
- **Trailing spaces** differ: MySQL 8 default collations are NO PAD (`'abc' = 'abc  '` is FALSE); SQL Server pads (`TRUE`). Older MySQL collations such as `utf8mb4_general_ci` pad.
- Force a case-sensitive compare: MySQL `col COLLATE utf8mb4_bin = 'x'` (or `BINARY col`); SQL Server `col COLLATE Latin1_General_CS_AS = 'x'`.
- Normalise before comparing or deduping: `LOWER(TRIM(email))`. Remember plain `TRIM` removes spaces only, not tabs or newlines in either engine (use `REPLACE(col, CHAR(9), '')`, or pass the characters explicitly to `TRIM`).
- Standard dedupe pattern: group by the cleaned key and keep `MIN(id)`.

examples.title: Find duplicate accounts after cleaning
examples.explain_md: Customers 4 and 6 only collide once the email is lower-cased and trimmed. Grouping on the raw column would see two different values (the trailing space).
examples.mysql: SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email, COUNT(*) AS accounts, MIN(customer_id) AS keep_id FROM customers GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY clean_email;
examples.tsql: SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email, COUNT(*) AS accounts, MIN(customer_id) AS keep_id FROM customers GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY clean_email;

examples.title: Case-insensitive and trailing-space equality
examples.explain_md: Default collation matches 'PABLO@mail.org' (customer 4) for a lower-case literal, but customer 6's value has a trailing space.
examples.mysql: SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers WHERE email = 'pablo@mail.org' ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers WHERE email = 'pablo@mail.org' ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: MySQL 8 (NO PAD collation) returns only customer 4. Real SQL Server ignores trailing spaces in `=` and returns customers 4 and 6 - use `LIKE` or `RTRIM` if you need the difference.

examples.title: LIKE is case-insensitive by default
examples.explain_md: Pattern `'pablo%'` matches 'PABLO@mail.org' and 'pablo@mail.org ' in both engines.
examples.mysql: SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers WHERE email LIKE 'pablo%' ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers WHERE email LIKE 'pablo%' ORDER BY customer_id;

pitfalls_md: `WHERE LOWER(col) = 'x'` is redundant under a CI collation and blocks index use; apply LOWER only when the collation is case-sensitive or when building a cleaned key.
`LIKE '%x'` (leading wildcard) cannot use an index in either engine.
